newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen rebel leaders set to return to Grozny.
newsitem.headline: Chechen rebel leaders set to return to Grozny.

text.p: Chechen rebel leaders are due to appear openly in the capital Grozny on Tuesday for the first time since they lost it to Russian troops in early 1995, to discuss the formation of a new regional government.

Interfax news agency said separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov and other top rebels would take part in a congress of political groups in Grozny, abandoned by both Russian troops and rebel fighters under a peace deal.

Maskhadov and Moscow envoy Alexander Lebed agreed terms in August to end 21 months of fighting, which killed tens of thousands of people, and defer by five years a decision on the most sensitive issue, the region's future political status.

Russia also agreed to withdraw most of the forces it sent in December 1994 to quell the separatist revolt in Chechnya. Russian troops have suffered a series of humiliating defeats and have failed to establish control over the whole of Chechnya.
The deal, said by Lebed to be a fair one with no winners or losers, has won conditional backing from President Boris Yeltsin, who is now vacationing outside Moscow before undergoing heart surgery.
But the agreement has in effect dumped Chechnya's pro-Moscow administration, led by Doku Zavgayev, and left most of the region in rebel hands in exchange for few concessions by the separatists.

Yandarbiyev has made clear he sees the five-year period agreed with Lebed as an opportunity for Russia to find a face-saving way to rubberstamp the region's independence rather than time for the rebels to reconsider their defiance of Moscow's rule.

Some top Russian officials, including Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov and influential Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov, have distanced themselves from Lebed, expressing varying degrees of doubts about the terms.
Interfax said Chernomyrdin and Lebed had met on Monday to discuss further plans on Chechnya. It gave no details.
Grozny is now guarded by joint patrols following the withdrawal of Russian troops and rebel forces.
The congress of about 20 mainly pro-rebel groups is being held just days after celebrations of the fifth anniversary of Chechnya's declaration of independence.
Interfax did not say whether the Chechen separatist leaders planned to be in Grozny only for the congress or whether they meant to establish a permanent presence in the devastated city.
It quoted a senior rebel source as saying the congress would discuss how to create a new Chechen government which could be formed this autumn.

Lebed says Chechnya should have a coalition cabinet to avoid civil war between the rebels, who control the south of the region, and their rivals, who are strong in the north and some parts of central Chechnya.
But the rebels have made clear they mean to form their own cabinet incorporating representatives of other political groups and including some members of Zavgayev government.
Interfax quoted Ruslan Kutayev, a leading participant of the Grozny conference, as saying the rebels had reserved up to 10 seats in the government for other parties.
Kutayev said "professionals and experts" from Zavgayev's government would be welcomed into the new cabinet. He said three of Zavgayev's aides had already been invited.

Zavgayev, who is currently in Moscow, has accused Lebed of staging a coup d'etat and surrendering Chechnya to the separatists. He says his cabinet is based in the town of Urus Martan in central Chechnya and has no plans to stop functioning.
